analysis.evidence: The verb links שָׂרַי (Sarai) to עֲקָרָה (barren). The following clause אֵין לָהּ וָלָד (she had no child) clarifies her condition.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וַ precedes a Qal wayyiqtol, third-person feminine singular, agreeing with שָׂרַי.
analysis.sense: to be in a state or condition

evidence.note: The verse explicitly gives Sarai as the name of Abram’s wife.
God identifies שָׂרַי as Abraham’s wife and gives her the name שָׂרָה.
Kings and their noblewomen appear in parallel. The noun for the women, שָׂרוֹת, is the plural of שָׂרָה.

article.name: שָׂרַי
article.summary: Sarai is the name by which Abram’s wife is introduced. Her later name שָׂרָה has the same form as the Hebrew noun for a princess or noblewoman, supporting a similar meaning for Sarai. The text leaves the force of the earlier name’s ending unexplained.

draft.definition: Sarai, the earlier name of Abram’s wife Sarah.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:29 names Abram’s wife Sarai. Genesis 17:15 gives both names when God tells Abraham to call her Sarah.

analysis.evidence: Genesis 11:29 names Abram’s wife שָׂרַי. Verse 30 repeats her name, describes her as עֲקָרָה ‘barren’, and says אֵין לָהּ וָלָד ‘she had no child’.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal name with no prefix or suffix. It is the subject of the feminine singular verb וַתְּהִי.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Abram’s wife before she was named Sarah.

analysis.evidence: In אֵין לָהּ וָלָד, לָהּ identifies Sarai as the possessor and וָלָד means “child.” The clause says “she had no child,” explaining the preceding description of Sarai as barren.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew negative existential particle in the form אֵין, with no attached prefix or suffix.
